entities.summary:
The Battle of Ain Jalut was a pivotal clash between the Egyptian Mamluk Sultanate and the Mongol Empire that took place on September 10, 1260, in the Well of Harod, marking a turning point in the history of the Middle East and the Mediterranean. This decisive victory for the Mamluks halted the Mongol conquests in the region and preserved Islamic dominance in the Middle East, shaping the course of Islamic history and the development of the Mamluk Sultanate. The consequences of the battle were far-reaching, as it led to the decline of the Mongol Empire's power in the region and paved the way for the rise of the Mamluk Sultanate, which would go on to play a significant role in the politics of the Middle East for centuries to come.

The battle itself was a bloody and intense clash between the two armies, with the Mongols suffering heavy casualties and their leader, Kitbuqa, being killed in the fighting. The Mamluks, led by Sultan Baibars, emerged victorious, but at great cost, with estimates suggesting that up to 20,000 men were killed in the battle. The aftermath of the battle saw the Mamluks consolidate their power in the region, while the Mongols were forced to retreat and regroup.

The legacy of the Battle of Ain Jalut can be seen in the long-term consequences of the battle, including the preservation of Islamic dominance in the Middle East and the rise of the Mamluk Sultanate. The battle also marked a turning point in the history of the Mongol Empire, as it halted their conquests in the region and led to a decline in their power. In the words of historian, Bernard Lewis, 'The Battle of Ain Jalut was a major turning point in the history of the Middle East, marking the end of the Mongol threat and the beginning of a new era of Islamic dominance.'

In the end, the Battle of Ain Jalut was a defining moment in the history of the Middle East, one that would have far-reaching consequences for the region and its people.
